summary: Proposes an ietf URN namespace for naming IETF documents, including RFCs, STDs, FYIs and BCPs, and the minutes of working group and BOF meetings.

eli5.summary: A way to give each RFC and meeting record a permanent name tag that never changes, whatever the website address.

questions: what is the ietf urn namespace
how do i write a urn for an rfc
subtitle: A permanent, location-independent name for RFCs, STDs, FYIs, BCPs, Internet-Drafts and IETF meeting minutes, such as urn:ietf:rfc:2141.

tldr.problem: A Uniform Resource Name (URN) system has to support new naming systems, and IETF documents had no URN namespace of their own.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2648 registers the formal URN namespace ietf. A name is urn:ietf: followed by a series prefix (rfc, fyi, std, bcp, id or mtg) and a number or string, defined with an ABNF grammar and resolved through mirrored copies of the documents.
tldr.outcome: Each assigned name is persistent and never reassigned, even though the underlying document may change. The memo is Informational and has been updated by RFC 6924 and RFC 9141.

today: RFC 2648 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 6924 and RFC 9141; read those alongside it for the current state of the ietf namespace.

sections.title: A Namespace for IETF Documents
sections.content:
A system for Uniform Resource Names (URNs) must be able to support new naming systems. RFC 2648 serves as an example of proposing one: the ietf namespace.

The namespace covers the RFC family of documents (RFCs, STDs, FYIs and BCPs) published by the RFC Editor, the minutes of working group (WG) and birds of a feather (BOF) meetings held at IETF conferences, and the Internet Drafts published by the Internet Drafts Editor. It is a formal namespace, and the current URN framework and URN syntax support it.
sections.eli5: It sets up a special list of permanent names for the IETF's papers and meeting notes.

sections.title: The Name Syntax
sections.content:
The registration template gives the namespace ID ietf, registration version number 1 and registration date 1999-04-22. The part after urn:ietf: (the namespace specific string) is defined in ABNF as one of: rfc:, fyi:, std: or bcp: followed by digits; id: or mtg: followed by a string; or another string with a different prefix, kept for future expansion. A string is one or more digits, letters or hyphens.

The whole URN is case-insensitive, and no additional characters are reserved. The RFC warns that the grammar must be updated if the IESG adds a new document series or if a working group or BOF uses characters outside that range, so any resolver should be written knowing this can happen at any time.
sections.eli5: A name has a fixed shape: first the club name, then what kind of paper it is, then its number or title. Capital letters do not matter.

sections.title: Uniqueness, Persistence and Assignment
sections.content:
Names are unique because the RFC Editor assigns each RFC number uniquely. STDs, FYIs and BCPs do not map one-to-one onto RFCs, so the RFC Editor's index files (rfc-index.txt, fyi-index.txt, bcp-index.txt, std-index.txt) are the definitive statement of which names exist. Meeting minutes URNs are unique because they include the sequence number of the IETF conference, and the Internet Drafts editor's 1id-abstracts.txt is definitive for drafts.

Persistence is separate from document changes. A URN, once assigned, is never reassigned to a different resource. Whether a document itself can change is at the RFC Editor's discretion: STDs, FYIs and BCPs may be composites of one or more RFCs, and that set may change over time.

Names are assigned in three ways: when the RFC Editor publishes a new RFC, FYI, STD or BCP; when a working group or BOF files minutes at an IETF conference; and when the Internet Draft Editor publishes a new draft.
sections.eli5: Once a name is given out it is never given to something else, even if the paper it points to gets updated or combined with others.

sections.title: Resolving the Names
sections.content:
To resolve these URNs, a mirrored copy of the underlying documentation is required. Resolution over HTTP is done by a set of simple Perl cgi-bin scripts, shown in Appendix A as example resolvers: one that maps a URN to a citation (called I2C) and one that maps a URN to a URL (called I2L).

The scripts look up RFC, FYI, STD and BCP numbers in the index files named above, and meeting names using a table that maps IETF conference numbers to dates. Anything unrecognized gives an error such as 400 Bad Request or 404 Not Found.

The RFC lists four example names a resolver can handle.
sections.eli5: A permanent name is only useful if something can turn it into a real place to read. The memo includes small example programs that look the name up in the official lists.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The namespace defines no additional reserved characters, so it adds no security considerations beyond those of the reserved characters in the URN syntax specification, RFC 2141. None of those reserved characters are used in the namespace specific string.

Resolvers may therefore be considered secure in the sense that any escaping of characters in that string MUST cause the resolver to report incorrect syntax.
sections.eli5: Because the names only use plain letters, numbers and hyphens, there is little room for trick characters. A name with odd escapes is simply rejected.

references.text: Crocker, D. and P. Overell, "Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF", RFC 2234, November 1997.
